About

I study economics at Stanford and co‑founded Verdnt Group.

Next summer I’ll join DRW’s central strategy team in Chicago.

I’m also interested in computer science and philosophy, and I like understanding what people value and how they put ideas to use.

Building

Verdnt Group

I co-founded Verdnt Group with Diego Sanchez Tirado. We’re building Verdnt Studio, a tool for food and drink teams developing new drinks. The goal is to help them turn market research into product ideas they can test.

Co-founder

More on Verdnt Studio

Verdnt Studio pulls its research from social media and retail shelves. I work with clients to understand what they need and build the software.

Our client work includes software that combines market research with a company’s product information to suggest new products. Teams can check the sources behind each suggestion before deciding what to test.

Visit Verdnt Group

Trus

I co-founded Trus with Diego Sanchez Tirado to help people create software for their own work. The idea was to describe what you needed and have AI build a workspace for it. Trus is now retired.

Co-founder · Retired

How Trus worked

I helped build the first version, where AI assembled workspaces from a set of tables, charts, calendars, and other components we had built.

I later focused on product direction and finding customers, while Diego led the engineering.

Deciding with incomplete data

I rarely have all the data I want when I need to decide, and waiting usually doesn’t fix that. So I pick a path and say why. Then I note the risks and what I’ll check next.

Free will and Statesman

The rule in Statesman, my board game, is “no fate, only action and reaction.” I think about my own choices roughly the same way. My philosophy essays keep coming back to the idea that a choice can be voluntary and still be shaped by past experience. Schopenhauer wrote, “Man can do what he wills but he cannot will what he wills.”

Tech & AI

On my own time, I run a small team of AI agents that handle my coding and notes.

How my agents are organized

I run my agents with a supervisor and workers assigned to specific tasks. Each worker gets a separate copy of the project to work in, so concurrent changes stay isolated. I route difficult or ambiguous work to stronger models and use lighter ones for small, clear tasks. If a simple task fails verification twice, I move it to a stronger model.

From: how my agent fleet is organized

What I expect back

I want work carried through to a usable result. An agent should finish the task and check what it tells me against the actual system and my earlier decisions, even when the report came from another agent. When something fails, I want a straight answer with enough evidence to understand why, and I want to hear when an idea isn’t worth doing.

From: the feedback I give my agents

Prove it works

I ask agents to prove UI changes by using the app through its actual interface, following the project’s verification steps. An end-to-end test means following real items from every input to the final output, with counts at each step that explain where items ended up, including anything held or rejected. Empty or broken inputs need checking too.

From: how I verify product changes

Keep the system current

When I change a rule, I want the tools and instructions around it updated too, including work already in the queue. I keep decisions and project context in files that agents can consult, with a current handoff so another tool can pick up the work. I will change the architecture when the output needs it, and I want a change reverted if the result gets worse.

From: changing rules across connected workflows

Let the bots handle the clicks

I want bots to handle routine dashboard steps they can do themselves. I keep the questions that involve unclear goals or real tradeoffs.

From: deciding what to automate

My Camber quoting demo

In a quoting product, a wrong answer costs real money. A language model is good at reading a messy part description, so it does that part. The pricing math is plain code, with a check that flags when something went wrong. A model can sound sure and still be wrong, so when the demo gets a deliberately vague request, it answers “REVIEW REQUIRED.”

From: Camber, 2026

Explaining the tools I build

At Morgan Stanley, the agents I built were only useful once analysts understood how they worked. I spent as much effort explaining them to non-technical colleagues as I did on the code. At Verdnt, every suggestion shows its sources.

From: Morgan Stanley and Verdnt Group

Silent drops in my job-search pipeline

Almost every bug in the job-search pipeline I built was a silent drop. A source broke or a filter was too strict, and a real posting never showed up. Reading the results didn’t catch these, so I started checking for postings that should have been there.

From: a personal automation project, 2026

The Stanford memo

I want to build AI that helps people do more. In the winning Stanford policy memo I co-wrote, our part proposed short in-person checks where students explain their reasoning out loud.

From: philosophy coursework and the Stanford memo, 2026

Design

Make the purpose obvious

I like clean interfaces where I can tell what the product does. I want the visual style to make the next action easy to find.

From: the feedback I give on app design

Show me the choice

I ask to see substantial plans visually, with annotations. When something needs my judgment, I want clear options and a recommendation so I can see the tradeoff.

From: how I review plans and decisions

Keep the words plain

I ask for writing that gets to the point and sounds like a person. I want the result explained first, with the details needed to understand it.

From: my instructions for writing and agent replies

Consider the phone separately

I treat the phone layout as its own design problem. I want the content to stay usable when motion is reduced or JavaScript is off.

From: building this site

Books

Books I’ve read and still think about.

My Brilliant Friend

Elena and Lila have no family or legal tie, and they keep choosing to stay friends. Ferrante gives a lot of weight to what they leave unsaid.

Elena Ferrante · my favorite novel

Diagnostic Political Philosophy

Sluga asks how to make good decisions without the full picture, especially in politics with a lot of misinformation around. Economics raised the same question for me.

Hans Sluga · I helped research and edit it

Beyond Good and Evil

I read it in weekly meetings across a desk from Professor Sluga. He always had another question, so I made sure I’d done the reading before I came in.

Friedrich Nietzsche · read with Hans Sluga

The Order of Things

I helped build more than 200 pages of material for Sluga’s graduate seminar on it. I broke hard ideas into steps a graduate student could follow.

Michel Foucault · seminar material

Three books on meritocracy

I read them side by side for a Stanford writing class, and I still don’t know what merit should be. In all three, institutions keep changing what counts as merit, and the definition decides who wins. Kirn also writes about the gap between performing competence and having it.

Sandel, The Tyranny of Merit · Markovits, The Meritocracy Trap · Kirn, Lost in the Meritocracy

Republic and Apology

Statesman, the board game I designed, is based on Plato’s city run by philosopher-kings. I also still think about the allegory of the cave and the case for the examined life.

Plato · UChicago summer program, 2022
